Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 1:

(p-54) Surat al-Muddaththir is Meccan, and its verses number fifty-six.

﴿O you who are wrapped up!﴾ That is, al-mutadaththir (the one who has wrapped himself), who is wearing the dithar (dithār), which is what is worn over the shi'ar (shiʿār, the garment worn next to the body). It is said: this is the first surah to be revealed.

It is narrated from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was on Mount Hira', and I was called, 'O Muhammad, you are the Messenger of Allah.' I looked to my right and to my left and saw nothing. Then I looked above me, and there he was, sitting on a throne between heaven and earth — meaning the angel who had called me. I was terrified and returned to Khadijah and said, 'Wrap me up, wrap me up!' Then Gabriel descended and said: ﴿O you who are wrapped up!﴾" And from al-Zuhri: "The first thing revealed was the surah 'Read' up to His saying, ﴿what he did not know﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) grieved and began to climb the peaks of the mountains. Gabriel, peace be upon him, came to him and said, 'You are the Prophet of Allah.' So he returned to Khadijah and said, 'Wrap me up and pour cold water over me.' Then Gabriel descended and said, 'O you who are wrapped up!'" It is said that he heard from the Quraysh what he disliked, so he was saddened and covered himself with his garment, reflecting as a sorrowful person does, and he was commanded to leave off warning them, even if they heard it and harmed him. It is also said that he was asleep, wrapped up. It is also said that what is meant is one wrapped in the garment of prophethood and divine knowledge.

It was also read as (al-muddaththar), in the form of the passive participle from dathharahu, meaning: the one upon whom this great matter has been wrapped and with which he has been girded. In the reading of Abu al-Mundhir it is "O you who are wrapped up" (al-mutadaththir), in its original form.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 2:

﴿Arise﴾: that is, from your bed; or, arise with the resolve and determination of one who is set on the matter. ﴿And warn﴾: that is, carry out the warning and bring it into being. It has been said: warn your people, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen﴾. Or [warn] all of mankind, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a bringer of good tidings and a warner to all mankind﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 3:

﴿And your Lord, glorify([1])﴾ The word "your Lord" is singled out for magnification (takbir), which is the attribution to Him, exalted is He, of greatness (kibriya') in belief and in speech. It is related that "when it [the revelation] descended, the Messenger of Allah said: 'Allahu Akbar,' and Khadijah magnified [God] too, rejoiced, and became certain that it was revelation." It may also be understood as referring to the takbir of the prayer. The fa' (in fakabbir) carries the sense of a conditional, as if it were said: "Whatever has happened, then do not leave off magnifying Him." Or it indicates that the primary purpose of the command to stand up is that he magnify his Lord and declare Him free from association (shirk), for the first thing that must be known is the Creator, exalted is His majesty, and then His transcendence above whatever is unbecoming to His presence.

[1] Here the Arabic word فَكَبِّرْ (fakabbir), meaning "then magnify," is discussed; the verse as rendered reads: "And your Lord, then magnify."

﴿And your garments, purify﴾ from what is not pure. For it is obligatory in prayer, the first and foremost, and more desirable at other times. This is by keeping them clear of impurities and washing them after they become soiled, and also by shortening them, for their length leads to dragging their trailing parts over filth. This was the first thing he (ﷺ) was commanded to do: to abandon blameworthy customs. It is also said: it is a command to purify the soul from actions that are loathed and from states that are abhorred. It is said: "So-and-so has a pure hem and sleeves" when they describe him as free from faults and from stains of character.

﴿And abandon the punishment﴾. That is, abandon the punishment by remaining steadfast in forsaking what leads to it of sins. It is also recited (qira'ah) with a kasra on the الرّاءِ, and both are dialectal forms (lughatan), like الذُّكْرِ and الذِّكْرِ.

Surah 74, verse 6:

﴿And do not bestow, seeking more﴾ — i.e., do not give while seeing what you give as much, or seeking the greater in return. It is forbidden to give while hoping that the recipient will repay you with more than what you gave, though this is permissible. From this is the hadith: "The one who gives gifts for a return is rewarded for his gift." So the prohibition is either for prohibition (tahrim), and it is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because Allah Most High chose for him the noblest character and the best manners; or it is for disapproval (tanzih) for everyone. It is also read as (tastakthir) with a sukun, considering the state of pause (waqf), or as a substitution for "tamnun," as if it were said: "Do not bestow and do not seek more," meaning that it derives from the mann (favour, reproach) in the Almighty's words: ﴿a favour and no harm﴾, because whoever reproaches for what he gives regards it as much and counts it great. It is also read in the accusative (tastakthira), with "an" implied and its governing effect retained, like the saying of the one who said:

Ala ayyuhadha al-zajiri ahdura al-wagha
(Ah, you who restrain me, let me attend the battle)

It is also read with the "an" stated. In the reading in the nominative, it is permissible to delete "an" and its governing effect is nullified, as in the narration "ahduru al-wagha" in the nominative.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 7:

﴿And for your Lord﴾ i.e., for His sake, may He be exalted, or for His command.

﴿Then be patient﴾. Patience is enjoined without specification. It was said: it is patience over the harm of the polytheists; it was said: it is patience in performing the obligatory duties.

﴿Fa-idha nuqira fi al-naqur﴾ means: that is, the Trumpet is blown (nufikha fi al-sur). It is an agent noun (fa'il) from al-naqr (striking), in the sense of producing a sound (al-taswit). Its original meaning is the striking that is the cause of the sound. The fa' (fa) here indicates causation (al-sababiyya), as if it were said: "Be patient with their harm, for before them is a terrible day, on which they will encounter the consequence of their harm, and you will encounter the consequence of your patience with it." The element governing "idha" is what is indicated by the words of the Exalted: [the following clause]

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 74, verses 9–10:**

﴿That, that Day, will be a difficult day﴾ for the disbelievers. "That" (*dhalika*) is a demonstrative referring to the time of the trumpet blast (*al-naqr*). The sense of distance in it, despite the recent mention of what it points to, serves to signal the great remoteness of its rank in terror and severity. It is in the nominative case by way of inception (*ibtida'*), and "*yawma'idhin*" (that day) is a substitute (*badal*) for it, built on the vowel *fatha* (*mabni*, indeclinable) because it is attached to a non-declinable word. The predicate (*khabar*) is "*yawmun 'asirun*" (a difficult day).

It was also said that "*yawma'idhin*" is an adverbial complement (*zarf*) of the predicate, the intended sense being: "That time is the occurrence of a difficult day." And "*'ala*" (upon) is connected to "*'asir*" (difficult). It was also said that it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier of "*'asir*," or as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the pronoun concealed within it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿not easy﴾ is an emphasis on its difficulty for them, implying its ease for the believers.

Scholars differed over whether the intended reference is the first blast or the second. The correct view is that it is the second, since its severity is specific to the disbelievers. As for the first blast, its ruling, which is the stunning (*is'aq*), encompasses both the righteous and the wicked, although it is said to be specific to those who are alive at the time it occurs.

Reports have come that there are holes in the Trumpet (*al-Suwar*) equal in number to all the souls, and that these souls will be gathered into those holes at the second blast. At the blast, from each hole a soul will emerge to the body from which it was taken, and the body will return to life by the permission of Allah, Exalted is He.

﴿That, that Day, will be a difficult day﴾ for the disbelievers. "That" (*dhalika*) is a demonstrative referring to the time of the trumpet blast (*al-naqr*). The sense of distance in it, despite the recent mention of what it points to, serves to signal the great remoteness of its rank in terror and severity. The predicate (*khabar*) is "*yawmun 'asirun*" (a difficult day).

It was also said that "*yawma'idhin*" is an adverbial complement (*zarf*) of the predicate, the intended sense being: "That time is the occurrence of a difficult day." And "*'ala*" (upon) is connected to "*'asir*" (difficult). It was also said that it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier of "*'asir*," or as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of the pronoun concealed within it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿not easy﴾ is an emphasis on its difficulty for them, implying its ease for the believers.

Scholars differed over whether the intended reference is the first blast or the second. The correct view is that it is the second, since its severity is specific to the disbelievers. At the blast, from each hole a soul will emerge to the body from which it was taken, and the body will return to life by the permission of Allah, Exalted is He.

﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and it may refer back to either of two pronouns. It may refer to the ي in ذَرْنِي, meaning: leave Me alone with him, for I will suffice you in taking vengeance on him. Or it may refer to the ت in خَلَقْتُ, meaning: I created him alone, and no one shared with Me in his creation. Or it may refer to the omitted returning pronoun (al-ʿāʾid al-maḥdhūf), meaning: and the one whom I created solitary, unique, having no wealth and no child.

It was said that it was revealed concerning al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra al-Makhzūmī, who was called "the Solitary" (al-Waḥīd) among his people. So this is mockery of him and of his nickname, and a turning of him away from the praise his people intended for him toward dispraise, by describing him as solitary in regard to wealth and children, or solitary from his father, since he was an illegitimate son (zanīm), as has passed, or solitary in wickedness.

﴿And I granted him extensive wealth﴾: spread out, abundant, or extended with increase, from "madda al-nahr" (the river extended), and another river extended it. It was said: he had livestock, crops, and trade. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that it was the various kinds of wealth he had between Makkah and al-Ta'if. It was also said that he had in al-Ta'if a garden whose fruit never ceased, in summer or winter. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said he had a thousand dinars (gold coins). Qatadah said six thousand dinars. Sufyan al-Thawri said four thousand dinars. Al-Thawri also said one million dinars.

Quran 74:13 "And sons attending (him)": present with him in Mecca, enjoying the sight of them; they never leave him, either for managing work or trade, since they were self-sufficient owing to their abundant blessings and large number of servants; or present at assemblies and gatherings because of their standing and prominence. It is said: he had ten sons; it is said: thirteen; it is said: seven, all of them men: al-Walid ibn al-Walid, Khalid, 'Imarah, Hisham, al-'As, al-Qays, and 'Abd Shams. Three of them embraced Islam: Khalid, Hisham, and 'Imarah.
And I made [his] path smooth for him, a smooth making. And I spread out for him leadership and wide standing, until he was called "the basil of Quraysh."

Then he hopes that I will add more ﴿to it﴾, beyond what I have given him. This is a denial and a rejection of his greed and eagerness, either because there is no increase possible upon what he has been given in abundance and plenty, or because it contradicts his condition of ingratitude for blessings and his obstinate opposition to the One who bestowed them. It is also said that he used to say: "If Muhammad is truthful, then Paradise was created only for me."

"Nay," a rebuke and reprimand to him for his empty greed, and a severing of his frustrated hope. His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Indeed, he was stubborn toward Our verses﴾ is a causal explanation for that, by way of an assertive resumptive clause (al-isti'naf al-tahqiqi), for opposing the verses of the Benefactor despite their clarity, and denying His blessing despite its abundance, is something that necessitates his being wholly deprived. What he was given, he was given only as a gradual lead-on (istidraj). It was said: after the revelation of this verse, his wealth continued to diminish until he perished.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 17:

﴿I will overwhelm him with a rugged ascent.﴾ I will cover him with what he hopes for in place of more (of wealth), or [I will impose on him] an arduous steep path (ʿaqabah) of ascent, and this is a parable for the harsh, unbearable punishment he will meet with.

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿He will be required to climb an ascent (ʿaqabah) in the Fire. Whenever he places his hand upon it, it melts; when he lifts it, it returns. And whenever he places his foot, it melts; when he lifts it, it returns.﴾ And from him, upon whom be peace, ﴿al-Su'ud is a mountain of fire upon which he will climb for seventy autumns, then he will fall down from it, and so on forever.﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, he reflected and calculated.﴾ This is a justification for the threat and for his deserving it; or it is an explanation of his obstinacy toward the signs of Allah, the Exalted. That is: he reflected on what he should say concerning the Qur'an, and he determined in his own mind what he would say.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 19:

﴿He was killed; how he calculated!﴾ This is an expression of wonder at his calculation and his accuracy in it, regarding the aim that the Quraysh were targeting, may Allah fight them. Or it is praise of him in the manner of mockery toward him. Or it is a narration of what they repeated of their saying: "He was killed; how he calculated," as a sneering at them and at their admiration for his calculation and their magnifying of his words. The meaning of their saying, "May Allah kill him, how brave he is," or "May Allah disgrace him, how poetic he is," is the indication that he has reached the degree of bravery and poetry in a real sense, such that his envier invokes this against him.

It is narrated that al-Walid said to the Banu Makhzum: "By Allah, I have just heard from Muhammad a speech that is neither the speech of mankind nor the speech of the jinn. Indeed it has a sweetness, and upon it is a radiance, its upper part is fruitful and its lower part is abundant, and it rises high and nothing rises above it." Then the Quraysh said: "By Allah, al-Walid has become a Sabian! By Allah, all of the Quraysh will become Sabians." His nephew Abu Jahl said: "I will take care of him for you." So he sat by him, grieved, and spoke to him in a way that heated him up. Then he (al-Walid) stood and came to them and said: "You claim that Muhammad is a madman; have you seen him choke? You say he is a soothsayer; have you seen him practice divination? You claim he is a poet; have you seen him ever attempt poetry? You claim he is a liar; have you ever caught him in any lie?" They said to all of that: "No, by Allah." Then they said: "So what is he?" He reflected and said: "He is nothing but a sorcerer. Have you not seen that he separates a man from his family, his son, and his clients? And what he says is nothing but magic that he has transmitted from the people of Babylon." The assembly erupted with joy, and they dispersed, impressed by his words and marveling at them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 20:

(p-58) ﴿Then, may he be destroyed, how he measured!﴾ It is a repetition for emphasis (mubalaghah). "Thumma" (then) here indicates that the second [curse] is more intensive than the first, while in what follows it retains its original sense of temporal succession (tarakhi al-zamani).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 21:

﴿Then he looked﴾ — i.e., at the Qur'an, time and again, over and over.

**﴿Then he frowned﴾**: he contracted his face when he found in it no point to attack, and did not know what to say. It was also said: he looked at the faces of the people, then contracted his face. And it was said: he looked at the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then contracted his face toward him.

**﴿And scowled﴾**: *wabasar* is a follow-on (ittiba') to *'abasa* (he frowned), added for emphasis and rhyme.

Then he turned away from the truth, or from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

And he was arrogant, refusing to follow him.

﴿So he said, "This is nothing but magic that is transmitted (or learned)."﴾ That is: it is related and learned. The "fa" (فَ, "so") indicates that when this phrase occurred to his mind, he uttered it without hesitation or delay.

And His, exalted is He, saying:
"In this is nothing but the word of a human being" (Q. 74:25) is an emphatic restatement of what precedes it, and for this reason it is left without a conjunction (al-'atif).
﴿I will cast him into Saqar﴾ is a *badal* (substitute, or appositive) for "سَأُرْهِقُهُ صَعُودًا" (I will overwhelm him with a steep ascent).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 27:

﴿And what will make you know what Saqar is?﴾ That is: what thing informs you of what Saqar is? This is on the reading where the first "ma" (what) is a subject (mubtada'), and "adraka" (made you know) is its predicate (khabar), and the second "ma" is a predicate (khabar) as well, because it is the one that conveys what is intended in terms of awe-inspiring magnitude and horror. And "Saqar" is a subject (mubtada'), meaning: what is it in its description? This is as has been mentioned repeatedly, that "ma" may be used to ask about a quality, although the more common usage is to ask with it about the name and the reality (haqiqah).

And His, exalted is He, saying:

Quranic quotations: ﴿لا تُبْقِي ولا تَذَرُ﴾ = ﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾.

**Translation:**

﴿It leaves nothing and spares nothing﴾ is an explanation of its (Saqar's) description and state, and a fulfilment of the implicit promise hinted at by "And what will make you know what Saqar is?" It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "Saqar," but that is not the case. That is, it leaves nothing that is cast into it without destroying it, and when it has destroyed something, it does not leave it as a ruined thing until it is restored; or, it does not leave anything and does not let it be from destruction, rather everything that is thrown into it is certainly destroyed.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 29:

﴿Scorching to the human being.﴾ It alters the outer layer of the skin and blackens it. It has been said: it scorches the skin with a single blaze, leaving it blacker than the night. It has also been said: it is visible to people, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you will surely see it with the eye of certainty.﴾ It was also read as "lawwahatan" (scorching) in the accusative, by way of specification (al-ikhtisas) for the sake of awe-inspiring emphasis (al-tahwil).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 30:

﴿Over it are nineteen.﴾ That is: an angel, or a category, or a rank, or a chief among the angels who are in charge of it and who exercise authority over its inhabitants. It is also read with the vowelling of the letter ʿayn in "ʿashara" (ʿashara) left unvowelled (sukūn), to avoid a succession of vowels in what is in the ruling of a single word. It is also read as "tisʿatu aʿshur" (tisʿatu aʿshur), the plural of ʿashīr (ʿashīr, a companion or kinsman), like "yamīn" and "aymun" (yamīn and aymun, "right hand" in its singular and plural forms).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 31:

﴿And We have not made the companions of the Fire﴾, i.e., those who manage its affairs and are in charge of punishing its inhabitants,

﴿except angels﴾, so that they would be of a different kind from those being punished, and would neither show them mercy nor find comfort in them. For they are the strongest of creation, the most upright in upholding the right of God, Mighty and Majestic, and in being angry for His sake, exalted is He, and the most severe in might against the Prophet (ﷺ)'s enemies. Each one of them has the strength of both the two weighty ones (al-thaqalayn, i.e., humans and jinn). One of them drives the nation, with a mountain on his neck, and throws them into the Fire, and throws the mountain upon them. It is related that when ﴿Over it are nineteen﴾ was revealed, Abu Jahl said to the Quraysh: "Can each group of ten of you not overpower one man among them?" Then Abu al-Ashudd ibn Usayd ibn Kildah al-Jumahi, who was extremely strong, said: "I will suffice you against seventeen; you suffice me against two." Then it was revealed. That is: We have not made them men from your kind.

﴿And We have not made their number except as a trial for those who disbelieve﴾, i.e., We have not made their number except the number that became the cause of their being tempted into doubt, which is nineteen. Here the effect is expressed by the cause, to draw attention to the necessary connection between them. The meaning is not merely that God made their number that specific number in reality, but that He also made it so in the Qur'an, namely by the judgment that over it are nineteen. For through this their being tempted is realized, by their considering it on its own, their finding it strange that such a small number should be in charge of punishing most of the two weighty ones, and their mocking it, as has been mentioned. Upon this turns what follows concerning the certainty of the People of the Book and the increase of the believers in faith. They said: what specifies this number is that human souls differ in their reasoning and actions, due to the twelve animal faculties (al-quwa al-hayawaniyya) and the seven natural faculties (al-quwa al-tabi'iyya). Or: Hell has seven levels (darak), six of which are for the kinds of disbelievers, each kind being punished for abandoning belief, affirmation and action with types of punishment suited to it, and over each type is an angel, or a kind, or a rank that is in charge of it; and one level is for the sinners of this nation, who are punished in it for abandoning action with a type suited to it, in charge of which is one. Or: the hours are twenty-four, five of which are devoted to the five prayers, leaving nineteen, which may be turned to what one is held accountable for with types of punishment, in charge of which are the Zabaniyya (the angels of punishment).

﴿So that those who were given the Book may become certain﴾, related to the making, according to the meaning mentioned, i.e., that they may acquire certainty about his prophethood (ﷺ) and the truthfulness of the Qur'an, when they witness that what is in it agrees with what is in their own Book.

﴿And that those who believe may increase in faith﴾, i.e., their faith increases in quality, by what they see of the People of the Book's submission and their affirmation that it is so; or in quantity, by adding their faith in this to their faith in everything else that was sent down.

﴿And that those who were given the Book and the believers may not doubt﴾, a confirmation of what precedes it of certainty and the increase of faith, and a negation of whatever doubt might befall one who is certain. The believers were not placed in the same line as the People of the Book in the negation of doubt, since it was not said "and they may not doubt," in order to draw attention to the difference between the two negations in their state: the absence of doubt among the People of the Book accompanies what contradicts it, namely denial; the absence of doubt among the believers accompanies what requires it, namely faith, and how much is between them. Referring to them with the active participle after mentioning them with the relative pronoun and the verbal clause, which indicates occurrence, signifies the steadfastness of their faith after its increase and the firmness of their state in that.

﴿And that those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, i.e., doubt or hypocrisy, so this is a report of what would happen in Medina after the Hijra.

﴿And the disbelievers﴾, i.e., those who persist in denial.

﴿Say: What did God intend by this as an example?﴾, i.e., what did He intend by this number, which is so strange as to be an astonishing example? It was said: when they found it improbable, they supposed it was a parable struck. The singling out of this statement for the explanation, though it is of the kind of their temptation, is to indicate that it is independently shocking.

﴿Thus God leads astray whom He wills﴾. Dhalika (thus) refers to what precedes it of the meaning of leading astray and guidance. The position of the kaf (ka) originally is accusative, as it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar). The original construction is: God leads astray whom He wills.

﴿and guides whom He wills﴾, i.e., by leading astray and guidance that are like what has been mentioned of leading astray and guidance. The verbal noun is omitted, its adjective is put in its place, and then it is placed before the verb to convey restriction (qasr). The structure becomes: like that leading astray and that guidance, God leads astray whom He wills to be led astray, by turning his choice toward the side of error upon seeing signs that point toward the side of guidance; not a leading astray and guidance of a lesser degree than these two.

﴿And none knows the hosts of your Lord﴾, i.e., the multitudes of His creation, among which are the angels just mentioned.

﴿except Him﴾, since no one can enumerate the possible beings, or comprehend their realities and attributes, even in summary, let alone know the details of their conditions in quantity, quality and relation.

﴿And it is not﴾, i.e., Saqar, or the number of its guardians, or the verses that speak of its conditions.

﴿except a reminder to humanity﴾, i.e., except a reminder for them.

Kalla (﴿كَلا﴾) is a rebuke to those who denied it, or a denial and negation that they should have any remembrance.

﴿And by the moon﴾.

﴿By the night when it turns back﴾. It is also read: (إذا دَبَرَ, idha dabara), meaning the same as adbara (turned back), just as qabala means aqbala (came forward). From this is their saying: "They have become like yesterday of the abode" (ṣārū ka-amsi al-dār). It has also been said that it derives from dabira al-layl al-nahār, meaning when the night has left the day behind it.
﴿And by the dawn when it brightens﴾. That is: when it shines and becomes clear.

Surely it is one of the greatest (calamities).

It is an answer to the oath, or a reason for "kalla" (by no means), with the oath being a parenthetical insertion for emphasis. "Al-kubar" is the plural of "al-kubra" (the greatest). The feminine ending alif was treated like its taa', so just as the pattern "fu'latun" is pluralized as "fu'al," the pattern "fu'la" is pluralized as "fu'al" as well. A parallel is "al-qawasi'" as the plural of "al-qasi'a'" (the desert locust/ a kind of hard ground-dwelling form), as if it were the plural of "qasi'a." That is, (it is) one of the greatest calamities, meaning that the great calamities or the great misfortunes are many, and this one is unique in its magnitude, having no equal.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 36:

﴿Warner to mankind.﴾ It is a tamyiz (specification of the noun, indicating what is meant), meaning: "Indeed, it is one of the greatest (calamities) in warning." Or it is a hal (circumstantial accusative) of what the sentence indicates, meaning: "It has become great, warning." It has also been read as nadhir with a raf' (nominative), in which case it is a second predicate following the predicate of inna, or the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada').

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 37:

﴿For whoever among you wills to go forward or to lag behind﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "for mankind," meaning: a warner for whoever among you wills to hasten toward good, so that Allah the Exalted guides him, or does not will that, so that He leaves him astray. It has also been said that "for whoever wills" is the predicate (khabar) and "to go forward or to lag behind" is the subject (mubtada'), so that it carries the meaning of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 38:

﴿Every soul, for what it has earned, is held in pledge﴾ — mamrunatun ʿinda Allah taʿala bi-kasbiha (pledged with God, the Exalted, by its earning). Al-rahina (الرَّهِينَةُ, "the pledge") is a noun in the sense of al-rahn (الرَّهْنُ, "the pledging"), like al-shatima (الشَّتِيمَةُ, "the insult") in the sense of al-shatm (الشَّتْمُ, "the insulting"), and not an adjective (sifa). Otherwise it would have been said rahin (رَهِينٌ), because fa'il in the sense of maf'ul (مفعول) does not take the feminine ta' (التّاء).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 39:

﴿Except the companions of the right hand﴾ — they will be in gardens, asking one another about the guilty. They are those who, by what they did of good deeds, have freed their necks, just as a pledgor frees his pledge by paying the debt. It has been said: they are the angels. It has been said: they are the children. It has been said: they are those for whom the good reward (al-husna) from God the Exalted had already preceded. It has been said: they are those who were on the right of Adam, peace be upon him, on the Day of the Covenant (al-mithaq). It has been said: they are those who will be given their books in their right hands.

﴿In gardens﴾: it cannot be fully comprehended, and its description cannot be grasped. It is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), and the sentence is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that answers an implied question) arising from what precedes it, namely the exception of the People of the Right. It is as if it were said: "What is their state?" So it was answered: "They are in gardens." It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the People of the Right; that it is from their pronoun in His words, exalted is He, ﴿they question one another﴾; and that it is an adverbial complement (zarf) of the questioning. The intended meaning of their questioning is not that each of them asks another while each is simultaneously questioner and questioned. Rather, the questioning proceeds from them without its being directed at them. The form "al-tafa'ul" (التَّفاعُلِ), though originally established to indicate that an action proceeds from several parties and falls upon them together, such that each becomes both agent and object at once, as in your saying "تَراءى القَوْمُ" (the people saw one another), meaning each of them saw the other, nevertheless may be stripped of this second meaning, and it is intended to indicate only the first meaning. In that case the verb takes an object, as in your saying "تَراءَوُا الهِلالَ" (they sighted the crescent). Thus the meaning of ﴿they question one another﴾ is...

﴿Concerning the criminals﴾, they will ask them about their conditions. The object of the asking has been omitted, because it is the very same as the one being asked about.

And His, may He be exalted, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 42:

﴿What has brought you into Saqar?﴾ It is implied by a verb in the sense of "saying," which is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "they will ask one another": that is, they ask them, saying: "What has caused you to enter it?" So reflect upon this, and leave aside what the over-elaborators have strained themselves over in it.
They said, that is, the criminals, answering those who asked them: ﴿We were not among those who prayed﴾, meaning the obligatory prayers.

"And we used not to feed the needy"—understood as the continuous negation of feeding (lam nakun + present verb expressing sustained negation), not as the negation of continuous feeding, as has been mentioned repeatedly. And in it is an indication that the disbelievers are addressed with the subsidiary rulings (al-furu') with regard to being held accountable.

And we used to plunge into vain talk along with those who plunge into it.

Here, the verse reads: ﴿And we used to plunge along with those who plunge⁠﻿﻿ ﻿﻿⁠—⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠ into falsehood⁠﻿⁠﻿⁠﻿﻿⁠﻿ ... 

Let me correct and give the clean translation:

Abu al-Su'ud says: "We used to plunge (nakhudu, to engage in, to enter into) along with those who plunge (al-khaʼidin)," meaning: we would begin (nashra'u) in falsehood (al-batil) along with those who begin in it (al-shari'in fihi).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 46:

﴿And we used to deny the Day of Judgment﴾. That is, the Day of Recompense (al-jaza'). They attributed it to recompense (al-jaza'), even though it contains calamities and terrors without limit; because it is the most calamitous and the most terrifying of them, and because they were involved in it. The remainder of the calamities has passed, and the delay of their crimes, although these are greater than all of them, is for their magnification, as if they had said: "And we were, after all that, deniers of the Day of Judgment." And to show that their denial of it accompanied all their other enumerated crimes and continued until the end of their lives, as their statement indicates.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 47:

﴿Until there came to us the certainty.﴾ That is: death and its precursors.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 48:

﴿So the intercession of the interceders will not benefit them﴾ even if they all interceded for them. And the fa' (the particle "so/then," fa') in His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 49:

﴿So what is wrong with them that they turn away from the Reminder?﴾ The particle "fa" (so, therefore) indicates that the denunciation of their turning away from the Qur'an without any cause is consequent upon what precedes it, namely the things that necessitate turning towards it and being admonished by it, from the evil state of those who deny it. "Mu'ridin" (turning away) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase that functions as the predicate of "ma," which is interrogative, and "'an" (from) is connected to it. That is to say: if the state of those who deny it is as has been mentioned, then what has happened to them, turning away from the Qur'an, given the convergence of the things that necessitate turning towards it and the mutual pull of the incentives to believe in it? And the words of the Exalted:

﴿كَأنَّهم حُمُرٌ مُسْتَنْفِرَةٌ﴾ ﴿as if they were startled donkeys﴾ is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial qualifier, i.e. an accusative of state) of the concealed pronoun (*mustakinn*, the implied pronoun within the verb or participle) in "*Mu'ridīna*" (﴿turning away﴾), by way of *tadākhul* (overlapping or interweaving of the two elements). That is, they are likened to wild donkeys in flight, i.e. "*mushabbihīna bi-ḥumurin nāfiratin*" (likened to fleeing donkeys).

﴿They fled from a lion﴾. That is, from a lion. The word is on the pattern *fa'wala* (فَعْوَلَة), a noun form derived from *qasr* (القَسْر), meaning compulsion, subjugation and overpowering. It was also said that the *qaswara* are a group of archers who hunt them. The disbelievers are compared, in their aversion to the Qur'an and their turning away from its admonitions, to asses that bolt wildly in fright at something that startled them. In this comparison there is a clear condemnation of them and a denigration of their condition. And as for His statement, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 74, verse 52:

﴿Nay, every man among them desires that he be given scrolls spread open.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) with an implied element demanded by the context, as if it were said: They are not content with that reminder, nor do they accept it; rather, every one of them desires to be given parchments that are unrolled and read. This is because they said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "We will not follow you until you bring each of us books from heaven, whose address reads: From the Lord of the worlds to so-and-so son of so-and-so, in which we are commanded to follow you," just as they said: "We will not believe in your incantation until you bring down to us a book that we can read." It is also recited as (ṣuḥfan munsharah) with the ḥāʾ and the nūn pronounced with sukūn.

"Nay" (kalla) is a rebuke to them for that audacity. "Rather, they do not fear the Hereafter" (bal la yakhafuna al-akhirah), and therefore they turn away from the Reminder (al-tadhkirah), not because it is impossible for scrolls to be given to them.
Nay (﴿كَلا﴾): a rebuke for their turning away from it. ﴿Indeed, it﴾, that is, al-qurā, ﴿is a reminder﴾, and what a reminder it is!
﴿So whoever wills﴾ to remember it, ﴿remembers it﴾, and through it attains the happiness of both abodes.

[The Qur'an:] ﴿And they do not remember﴾ merely by their own will to remember, as is understood from the apparent meaning of His words, exalted is He: "So whoever wills, let him remember it" (74:55). For the will and desire of the servant have no influence on his actions. His words, exalted is He, ﴿unless Allah wills﴾ are an exceptive clause (istithna' mufarragh, "the exception in which the excluded element is left unstated, so the phrase takes its meaning from the context") from the most general categories. That is, "they do not remember for any cause among the causes, or in any state among the states, except by Allah's willing," or "in the state that Allah wills it." This explicitly states that the actions of the servants occur by the will of Allah, mighty and majestic. It has also been read as (tadhkurūna) in the second person, as an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person, "a change from speaking about them to addressing them directly"). It has also been read with both verbs in the intensive form (mushaddadan).

﴿He is worthy of piety﴾, meaning He is deserving that His punishment be feared, that He be believed in, and that He be obeyed.

﴿And worthy of forgiveness﴾, meaning He is deserving to forgive those who believe in Him and obey Him.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Muddaththir, Allah will give him ten good deeds for each number of those who affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ) and denied him in Makkah."
